questions.q: Why does the lesson argue a negative result needs the same methodological rigor as a positive one, rather than less?
options: Because negative results are legally required to have more seeds than positive results

Because a negative result is only informative if it genuinely rules out a well-specified hypothesis, which requires enough seeds, a fair baseline, and a properly tuned learning rate -- the same discipline a positive result needs
Because negative results are always easier to obtain than positive ones
Rigor doesn't matter for negative results since they don't get published
questions.explain: A sloppy negative result can't distinguish a real null effect from noise or an undertuned setup. The same rigor (seeds, fair baseline, LR tuning) that makes a positive result trustworthy is what makes a negative result a real finding rather than an artifact.

questions.q: What is the key difference between the claims "this doesn't work" and "I couldn't get this to work"?
options: There is no meaningful difference -- they mean the same thing

"This doesn't work" is a broader claim about the idea itself, earned only after ruling out bugs, undertuning, and scale limits, while "I couldn't get this to work" is a narrower, honest claim about a specific attempt that should name what wasn't ruled out
"I couldn't get this to work" is always the stronger, more rigorous claim
The distinction only matters for positive results, not negative ones
questions.explain: Conflating these is a common mistake. The narrower claim is honest about its limits and should explicitly state what wasn't tested (e.g. a wider hyperparameter sweep or larger scale), while the broader claim requires having ruled those things out.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what should be checked before reporting an experiment's outcome as a genuine negative result?
options: Whether the result would be popular with the team

The mundane explanations -- whether the baseline used the same data/budget, whether the new approach's learning rate was swept independently, and whether basic sanity checks (like overfitting a tiny batch) passed for the new code
Whether the experiment was run on a weekend or a weekday
Whether a senior researcher was present during the run
questions.explain: If the apparent negative result traces back to a mundane cause like an undertuned learning rate or a bug, it's actually a bug report, not a finding, and reporting it as a finding wastes a reader's time.

questions.q: Why might a method that needs a different learning rate than the baseline appear to 'not work' if evaluated using the baseline's learning rate?
options: Because learning rate has no effect on how a new method performs
Because the new method may require its own LR sweep to perform fairly, and evaluating it at the baseline's (possibly wrong-for-it) LR can make a genuinely viable method look broken
Because the baseline's learning rate is always optimal for every method
Because learning rate only matters for mixed-precision training
questions.explain: Different methods can have different optimal learning rates. Sweeping the LR independently for both the baseline and the treatment avoids mistaking an LR mismatch for a genuine negative result about the method itself.

questions.q: What distinguishes an effective negative-result write-up in terms of framing?
options: It avoids mentioning what was learned and focuses only on the time spent
It explicitly states what hypothesis or explanation got ruled out, framing the result as information gained rather than as time lost
It omits all methodological details to keep the write-up brief
It always recommends abandoning the research direction entirely
questions.explain: Framing a negative result around which hypothesis it rules out (e.g. 'this rules out explanation A, narrowing remaining hypotheses to B and C') turns it into a genuinely useful contribution rather than a report of wasted effort.
